binders: x and t are real spatial and temporal variables, and q(x,t) is a scalar concentration or density; this specializes the general real-valued system to m = 1 (printed page 1, explanation of (1.1) and paragraph preceding (1.2)).
ū is a fixed real transport velocity, constant in space and time in this example (printed page 1, constant-coefficient scalar discussion and paragraph preceding (1.2)).
f is the scalar flux function with defining formula f(r) = ūr, where r denotes its scalar argument rather than a new physical quantity (printed page 4, contaminant paragraph, f(q) = ūq).
x₁ and x₂ are arbitrary spatial endpoints in the integral balance (printed page 4, sentence preceding (1.10)).
hypotheses: A contaminant is carried by fluid through a one-dimensional pipe at constant velocity ū (printed page 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)).

Contaminant mass is conserved during transport; the selected homogeneous equation excludes the mass production or loss for which the source requires source terms (printed page 4, contaminant paragraph).
For passage from the integral balance to a classical differential equation, q and the composed flux f(q) must be sufficiently smooth (printed page 4, opening of section 1.1.2).
conclusions: The contaminant flux is f(r) = ūr (printed page 4, contaminant paragraph).

Conservation of contaminant mass with this flux yields the scalar advection equation q_t(x,t) + ūq_x(x,t) = 0, identified by the source as equation (1.2) (printed page 4, contaminant paragraph; printed page 1, (1.2)).

Specializing the stated integral balance to this flux gives d/dt ∫ from x₁ to x₂ q(x,t) dx = ūq(x₁,t) − ūq(x₂,t); this is a direct substitution into (1.10), rather than a separately displayed source formula (printed page 4, (1.10) and contaminant paragraph).
If contaminant mass is not conserved, the model must also contain source terms (printed page 4, end of contaminant paragraph).
definitions_and_conventions: q denotes concentration or density of contaminant, not the fluid velocity (printed page 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)).
Subscripts t and x denote partial derivatives with respect to time and space (printed page 1, explanation following (1.1)).
In (1.8), f(q(x,t))_x is the spatial derivative of the composed flux (printed page 3, (1.8)).
The integral of q between endpoints represents contaminant mass in that interval; its change equals the flux at x₁ minus the flux at x₂ (printed page 4, (1.10) and its explanatory paragraph).
implicit_context: The selected paragraph explicitly refers back to the scalar constant-velocity advection example, so its ū and q inherit their roles from page 1 (printed page 4, reference to (1.2); printed page 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)).
The flux identification is a scalar instance of the preceding observation that constant-coefficient linear systems have flux f(q) = Aq (printed pages 3–4, sentence spanning the page break).
The source distinguishes integral conservation from its classical differential expression when solutions lack sufficient smoothness (printed page 4, opening of section 1.1.2).

details: Mass inside an interval may change through endpoint transport even though contaminant mass is conserved; conservation does not assert that every interval has constant mass (printed page 4, explanation of (1.10)).
The balance uses f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)), fixing the order and sign of the endpoint terms (printed page 4, (1.10)).
The source specifies the exact flux f(q) = ūq, with no additive constant (printed page 4, contaminant paragraph).
The same constant ū appears as the transport coefficient in equation (1.2) and as the multiplier in the flux (printed page 1, (1.2); printed page 4, contaminant paragraph).
The selected claim concerns scalar contaminant transport under constant fluid velocity (printed page 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)).
Chemical reactions are an example of a mechanism requiring source terms when contaminant mass fails to be conserved (printed page 4, contaminant paragraph).

Preserve the scalar concentration or density interpretation of q and the constant velocity interpretation of ū (printed page 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)).
Preserve the equation q_t + ūq_x = 0 with the same coefficient as the flux (printed page 1, (1.2); printed page 4, contaminant paragraph).
Any included integral formulation must preserve the endpoint difference in (1.10), specialized using f(q) = ūq (printed page 4, (1.10) and contaminant paragraph).
Do not treat conservation as constant mass in each fixed interval: the source permits changes through endpoint flux (printed page 4, explanation following (1.10)).

Do not assert an unqualified classical differential consequence for nonsmooth q; the source explicitly conditions the integral-to-differential derivation on sufficient smoothness (printed page 4, section 1.1.2).

contract_plain_english: For a contaminant carried through a one-dimensional pipe at constant velocity ū, q(x,t) is its concentration or density and the flux is exactly f(q) = ūq (printed page 1, paragraph preceding (1.2); printed page 4, contaminant paragraph). Conservation of contaminant mass gives the advection equation q_t + ūq_x = 0, with the classical differential interpretation subject to the source's sufficient-smoothness proviso (printed page 1, (1.2); printed page 4, sections 1.1.1–1.1.2). The corresponding interval balance is the rate of change of interval mass equal to ūq(x₁,t) minus ūq(x₂,t), obtained by substituting the stated flux into (1.10). If contaminant mass is not conserved, source terms are required (printed page 4, contaminant paragraph).
